questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend using a Messages API tool call (run_sql_query) instead of asking Claude to write SQL in prose and parsing it out with a regex?
options: Regex parsing is faster than tool calling
A tool call returns the SQL as a structured tool_use block your code controls, instead of free text you have to extract and trust
Claude cannot generate SQL in plain text at all
Tool calls are required by the SQL standard
questions.explain: Tool use gives you a structured, parseable input (the sql field) rather than relying on fragile text extraction from a prose response.

questions.q: What does the 'description' field of the run_sql_query tool need to specify, per this lesson's real tool definition?
options: Nothing -- the input_schema alone is sufficient
That the connection is read-only and the tool should never be used for anything but SELECT
The user's name and email address
The exact row count the query will return
questions.explain: The description tells Claude what the tool does and its constraints -- here, that it's read-only and SELECT-only -- which shapes what kind of SQL the model generates.

questions.q: In the real round trip, what does Claude's response contain when it decides to query the database?
options: A tool_use block with the tool's name and a generated 'sql' input
A fully executed query result with no further code needed
A tool_result block
A plain-text SQL statement with no structure
questions.explain: Claude's reply carries a tool_use block naming run_sql_query and the generated SQL in its input -- your code then validates and executes it, and sends a tool_result back.

questions.q: Why does validate_sql() still matter even though the Lesson 9 database role has no write permissions?
options: It doesn't matter -- the read-only role alone is sufficient
It's a second, independent check that catches disallowed or malformed SQL in code, before it ever reaches the database driver
It replaces the need for a read-only role
It only checks for correct spelling in the query
questions.explain: Validation and the least-privilege role are independent layers -- validation catches problems in your own code path, while the role bounds what even a validated SELECT-shaped query could still do if something were missed.

questions.q: What must a schema-aware system prompt include so the model generates correct queries?
options: The user's IP address and browser version
The real table and column names in the database, so the model can't invent ones that don't exist
A list of every possible question a user might ask
The database administrator's password
questions.explain: Telling the model the actual schema -- real table and column names -- keeps it from hallucinating fields that aren't there, which is one of the most common natural-language-to-SQL failure modes.
